p: The man behind Ickworth was Frederick Hervey, the 4th Earl of Bristol, who was also Bishop of Derry. Work on the Rotunda started in the 1790s, and he planned it as a showcase for the art he'd collected on his travels around Europe. He never lived to see it finished, and the family completed the house in the decades after his death. It's an eccentric tale, and it explains a lot about why the place looks the way it does.

Inside, the grand rooms of the Rotunda are full of paintings, furniture and silver, but don't skip the basement. Ickworth's servants' quarters have been presented as they were in the 1930s, so you can see the kitchens and working spaces where staff kept the household running. Children often find it more fun than the posh rooms upstairs.

Allow half a day, more if you want a proper estate walk. The Albana Walk loops through the woods and gives you some lovely views across the park. Bring a picnic blanket and the dog, and pick a dry day if you can, as much of the joy is outdoors. The estate is reached from the village of Horringer, right by the gates.

Back in Bury St Edmunds, the abbey ruins and gardens are free to wander, St Edmundsbury Cathedral has its striking lantern tower, and the town is home to Greene King's Westgate Brewery, a big part of local life for generations. Add in a stroll round the market and you've got a really full day in this corner of Suffolk.
